title: Design Native Ads in an Email Inbox
followUps: Walk through what happens from the moment a user opens the inbox on Android to the moment an ad row is visible. What runs in parallel with loading the mail, and what happens if the ad service is slow?
A user dismisses an ad on their phone and opens the web inbox 5 seconds later. How does your design keep the ad from reappearing, and what consistency do you actually guarantee?

An advertiser is billed per click and claims a third of their clicks came from bots. How does your pipeline detect invalid clicks, and how does that interact with numbers the advertiser has already seen in their dashboard?
A campaign's daily budget is $5,000, but it's served from dozens of ad servers across three regions. How do you avoid overspending by a lot, or underdelivering, near the end of the day?
A lead-generation form submission contains the user's name and email for the advertiser. How do you handle it differently from impression and click events, and what privacy constraints apply?

interviewer.approach: Strong answers separate the latency-critical serving path from the high-volume, correctness-critical event path, and keep the inbox fast even when ads fail. Requirements: up to 2 ad slots per inbox load; ads must never delay mail rendering (fetched in parallel, rendered when ready, dropped after a timeout); targeting by coarse signals (location, language, declared interests, device) and never by email content; frequency caps per user per campaign per day; dismissals respected on every device; daily budgets and pacing; CPC and CPM pricing; lead forms; advertiser reports within ~15 minutes; exact daily billing with invalid traffic removed. Estimates: 300M DAU x ~10 inbox opens/day = 3B ad requests/day, ~35k/s average, ~100k/s peak; impressions ~4B/day (2 slots, some empty); clicks ~1% (~40M/day); events ~5B/day x ~300 bytes = ~1.5 TB/day raw. Serving: client calls an ad API in parallel with the mail fetch (or the inbox backend fans out with a ~50 ms budget); ad server loads a user profile (interests, caps, dismissals) from a low-latency store keyed by user id (e.g. Bigtable/Cassandra/Redis), retrieves eligible candidates from an in-memory index of active campaigns (targeting criteria -> campaign ids, refreshed from the campaign DB every few seconds), filters by caps, dismissals and budget state, scores with the click-prediction service (pCTR x bid = eCPM), runs a simple auction, and returns ad creatives plus signed tracking tokens. Creatives are pre-rendered into a client-agnostic schema (title, sender, body, form fields) so web, iOS and Android render natively; assets on a CDN. Cross-device: dismissals and impressions written to the user profile store (read-your-writes per user via a single home region or strongly consistent row); short client-side cache of dismissals as a fallback. Events: clients send impression/click/dismiss/form events with a unique event id and the signed token (prevents forged events, carries campaign/price); collected by an edge endpoint into Kafka; a stream processor deduplicates by event id, joins with serving logs, filters invalid traffic (rate per user/IP, bot signatures, click-without-impression), and writes per-campaign per-minute aggregates to an OLAP store for dashboards; a daily batch over the raw log produces the authoritative billing numbers (Lambda or Kappa architecture), with late events and invalid-click adjustments reconciled. Budget pacing: a central budget service tracks spend from the stream (seconds of lag) and hands each ad server a spend allowance or throttle probability; slight overspend is tolerated and not billed. Lead forms: submitted over a separate encrypted path, stored per advertiser with retention limits and user consent, never mixed into analytics logs. Privacy: no email content in targeting, user-level data access controls, data retention limits.
hints: What's the worst thing the ads system can do to the inbox? How do you make that impossible?
At 100,000 ad requests a second with a ~50 ms budget, what can you afford to look up per request, and what needs to be in memory already?
Where do frequency caps and dismissals live so that every device sees the same answer?
If the same click event arrives twice, or a bot sends 1,000 of them, what happens to the advertiser's bill?
Do the dashboard numbers and the invoice numbers have to come from the same computation? What does each need?
pitfalls: Fetching ads serially before rendering the inbox, or with no timeout, so ad problems slow down email.
Targeting on email content, or logging message data in ad events.
Querying the campaign database on every ad request instead of using an in-memory index refreshed in the background.
Counting events from client callbacks without event ids, signatures or deduplication, so retries and fraud inflate bills.
Billing directly from the real-time dashboard counters without a reconciled batch or invalid-traffic filtering.
Frequency caps and dismissals stored only on the client, so they don't carry across devices.
Per-server budgets with no central pacing, causing large overspend when a campaign is popular.
Treating lead-form submissions (personal data) like ordinary analytics events.
facts: About 300 million daily active users across web, iOS and Android; the average user opens the inbox about 10 times a day.
Up to 2 ad slots per inbox load. If no ad is ready in time, the slots are simply empty.
The inbox's own p99 render target is 300 ms on the server side; the ad decision must finish within about 50 ms at p99 or be dropped.
Targeting may use coarse location, language, device, account age and interests the user has declared or that come from ad settings. Email contents must never be used for targeting.
About 200,000 active campaigns at a time. Advertisers pay per click (most) or per thousand impressions, set daily budgets, and expect delivery to be spread over the day.
Frequency cap: by default a user sees the same campaign at most 3 times a day. A dismissed ad must not be shown again to that user on any device.
The click-through rate is about 1%. About 5% of ads include a lead-generation form; submissions go to the advertiser.
Advertisers want reports within about 15 minutes. Invoices are daily and must exclude invalid (bot or duplicate) traffic.
Events can arrive late: mobile clients batch events and may send them hours later after being offline.
Serving runs in three regions; a user is normally served from the nearest one.
deepDives: The serving path: candidate retrieval from an in-memory index, scoring, auction and the 50 ms budget
Frequency caps and dismissals consistent across devices
Event collection: signed tokens, event ids, deduplication and invalid-traffic filtering
Real-time reporting versus authoritative daily billing (stream plus batch reconciliation, late events)
Budget pacing across many ad servers and regions
